source: Week 3 of 'Weeks_1_to_4_-_DDoS_Detection_Project_UPDATED.docx' (group project document, 21 Oct 2026). Text copied from the document; nothing added except 'expected' (see direction_note).
hypothesis_note: The assumptions below are hypotheses. Where the data did not support an assumption, this is stated.
direction_note: 'Expected' is our reading of each assumption as a direction (higher / lower than benign, or just different), added only so the data can be compared with it. It is not in the Week 3 document; check it with the group. 'none' = the assumption states no direction for that column.
added_note: Features 8 to 11 were added after the first experiments, chosen for their security meaning. Notebook section 9c measures whether they help; nothing here claims that they do.

groups.raw_data: Packet count, byte count and timestamps of the first and last packet in the flow
groups.calculation: Packets (or bytes) divided by flow duration
groups.behaviour: How hard the source is pushing traffic. A flood aims to exhaust bandwidth or processing capacity, so its rate is high.
groups.assumption: Malicious flows in a flood send faster than normal user flows.
groups.lookalike: Yes. A large download, a video stream or a popular event can give similar rates.
groups.evasion: Yes. Slowing each source down lowers the rate, although this also lowers the damage per source.
notes: Data note: when the duration is zero the rate is undefined, and the dataset contains infinite and missing values here. This links to the cleaning step in Week 2.

groups.raw_data: Timestamps of the first and last packet
groups.calculation: Last packet time minus first packet time, in microseconds
groups.behaviour: Floods often produce very short flows (one request and no follow-up) or flows held open to tie up the server.
groups.assumption: Attack flows have a duration profile different from normal browsing.
groups.lookalike: Yes. Quick API calls are short, and file transfers or streams are long.
groups.evasion: Yes, by completing requests normally or closing connections at typical times.

groups.raw_data: Number of packets sent by the initiator and by the responder
groups.calculation: Tot Fwd Pkts divided by (Tot Bwd Pkts + 1). The +1 only avoids division by zero
groups.behaviour: A flood sends packets without waiting for replies, so the flow is one-sided, especially when the target is overloaded and stops answering.
groups.assumption: Benign flows are more balanced because both sides take part in the exchange.
groups.lookalike: Yes. Uploads, streaming and a server that is down for other reasons also give lopsided ratios.
groups.evasion: Partly. The attacker controls the traffic it sends, but not the replies, so the ratio can still change if the target struggles.

groups.raw_data: Timestamp of every packet in the flow
groups.calculation: Mean and standard deviation of the gaps between consecutive packets (either direction)
groups.behaviour: Attack tools send automatically, so gaps between packets may be very small or very regular.
groups.assumption: Human and normal application traffic is burstier and less regular.
groups.lookalike: Yes. Polling clients, heartbeat messages and other automated software are regular too.
groups.evasion: Yes, easily, by adding random delays.

groups.raw_data: TCP header flags of every packet
groups.calculation: Number of packets in the flow with the SYN flag set
groups.behaviour: Connection-opening floods send many SYN packets, so SYN counts are unusual relative to the rest of the flow.
groups.assumption: The HTTP-based attacks (LOIC-HTTP and HOIC) go through normal TCP connections, so the handshake flags carry some signal.
groups.lookalike: Yes. Busy servers see many connection openings from normal users.
groups.evasion: Yes, by completing connections properly or using a different protocol.
notes: Limitation: UDP has no TCP flags, so this feature says nothing about LOIC-UDP flows.

Data check (from the document): in the first runs the median SYN flag count is 0 for all three attack tools, and the first XGBoost model trained with a held-out tool did not use the feature at all. So this assumption is not supported so far. The group will decide whether to keep the feature after the feature comparison.

groups.raw_data: Length of each packet sent by the initiator
groups.calculation: Mean and standard deviation of those lengths
groups.behaviour: Attack tools often send fixed or repeated payloads, giving low variation in packet size.
groups.assumption: Normal requests vary more in size.
groups.lookalike: Yes. Machine-to-machine traffic such as API calls and monitoring pings is also uniform.
groups.evasion: Yes, by padding or randomising payloads.

groups.raw_data: Length of each packet sent by the responder
groups.calculation: Mean of those lengths (read from the CSV column Bwd Pkt Len Mean)
groups.behaviour: What the target sends back. A flood overwhelms the target, so its replies may be small, rare or missing.
groups.assumption: During an attack the target's replies are smaller or absent compared with normal exchanges.
groups.lookalike: Yes. Uploads, streaming, health checks and any server error also give small or empty replies.
groups.evasion: Not directly, because the attacker does not control the replies. The value reflects the target's state as much as the attacker's behaviour, so it may not carry over to other targets.

groups.raw_data: TCP header flags of every packet
groups.calculation: Number of packets in the flow with the RST flag set (RST Flag Cnt), and with the FIN flag set (FIN Flag Cnt)
groups.behaviour: How the connection is closed. Attack tools may abandon connections with a reset or never close them cleanly.
groups.assumption: Attack flows end differently from normal browsing.
groups.lookalike: Yes. Network faults, timeouts and impatient clients also produce resets, and short sessions often lack a clean close.
groups.evasion: Yes, by closing connections properly, which is cheap for HTTP floods.
notes: Limitation: UDP has no TCP flags, so these features say nothing about LOIC-UDP flows.

groups.raw_data: Number of packets sent by the responder; length of the packets sent by the initiator
groups.calculation: no_reply = 1 when Tot Bwd Pkts is 0, else 0. empty_payload = 1 when Fwd Pkt Len Mean is 0, else 0
groups.behaviour: Whether the exchange happened in both directions, and whether the flow carried any data.
groups.assumption: Many flood flows are one-sided or carry no application data, while most normal flows do both.
groups.lookalike: Yes. Port scans, failed connections, keepalives and one-way UDP traffic such as logging are also one-sided or empty.
groups.evasion: Yes, by sending real requests that get replies, at the cost of more effort per packet.
notes: Note: these indicators restate information already in the packet counts and lengths, so they may add little accuracy. They are included because they make explanations clearer.

groups.raw_data: Timestamp of every packet in the flow
groups.calculation: iat_cv = Flow IAT Std divided by (Flow IAT Mean + 1). The +1 only avoids division by zero
groups.behaviour: How regular the sending is, independent of how fast it is.
groups.assumption: Automated tools send at regular intervals, so the variation in gaps is small relative to the mean gap, while human traffic is burstier.
groups.lookalike: Yes. Polling clients, heartbeat messages and other automated software are regular too.
groups.evasion: Yes, easily, by adding random delays (the same weakness as feature 4).

dropped.title: Flows to the same destination in a window
dropped.assumption: The number of flows reaching a destination in a short window is much higher during an attack than in normal operation.
dropped.status: Dropped. The 21 February file (HOIC and LOIC-UDP) has no destination IP column, so this feature cannot be built for those tools. The model therefore judges each flow alone, which keeps the Week 1 limitation that a single flow cannot show many sources hitting one target.
